query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, degradation at elevated temperature is governed by whether a continuous, adherent, Al/Cr-rich oxide scale forms on the fcc matrix. Under oxidizing gas conditions, the formation of this protective oxide limits further oxygen ingress and suppresses deleterious phase changes, thereby preserving strength and fatigue properties. In contrast, exposure to reducing gas conditions inhibits the formation of a stable oxide scale, leading to internal oxidation and microstructural coarsening that accelerate degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a retained fcc matrix, demonstrating notable strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Expose nominally identical samples of the alloy to two controlled gas atmospheres (oxidizing vs. reducing) at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature exposure at a set high temperature for a defined duration, with one set of samples in an oxidizing atmosphere (high oxygen partial pressure) and another set in a reducing atmosphere (lower oxygen partial pressure) while all other parameters (e.g., heating rate, exposure time) are kept constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack) of a continuous, adherent Al/Cr-rich oxide scale on the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the Al and Cr in the alloy preferentially oxidize to form a protective scale that limits further oxygen diffusion into the substrate, thereby maintaining the integrity of the fcc matrix and its mechanical properties. In reducing conditions, because the oxygen activity is lower, this protective oxide does not form effectively; instead, internal oxidation and associated microstructural degradation (such as phase coarsening or localized compositional fluctuations) are promoted.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting-state baseline, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions are expected to show a thin, adherent Al/Cr-rich oxide layer, minimal internal oxidation, and only slight reductions in mechanical properties, whereas samples exposed to reducing conditions should exhibit more significant internal oxidation, microstructural coarsening, and a greater loss of mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy under ambient conditions without exposure to elevated-temperature test environments.
generation.boundary: The degradation mechanisms are evaluated under controlled high-temperature exposure with two discrete gas atmospheres: one with high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and one with substantially lower oxygen partial pressure (reducing), within the established time–temperature regime for accelerated oxidation or reduction testing.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative differences in degradation are supported by the proposed mechanism, the exact quantitative rate differences and the relative contribution of other synergistic elemental effects remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens. Expose one group to an oxidizing atmosphere (with a controlled high oxygen partial pressure) and the other group to a reducing atmosphere (with a controlled low oxygen partial pressure) at the same elevated temperature and for the same duration. After exposure, assess the surface oxide layer (using SEM/EDS or XPS), inspect the microstructure (using TEM/EBSD), and perform mechanical tests (such as yield strength and fatigue performance measurements).
measurements: Thickness and composition of the surface oxide scale
Extent of internal oxidation and microstructural coarsening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing atmosphere does not produce a continuous, protective Al/Cr-rich oxide scale (or if it results in equivalent or greater internal oxidation and degradation than the reducing atmosphere), or if the mechanical properties do not show a significant relative advantage compared to the reducing condition, then the hypothesis is falsified.
